name: Phentermine/Topiramate (Qsymia)
lead: Phentermine/topiramate extended-release (Qsymia) is a fixed-dose capsule combining phentermine, a sympathomimetic amine, with topiramate, an anticonvulsant, taken once daily to reduce appetite and increase satiety [2]. It was approved by the US FDA in 2012 for chronic weight management and in July 2022 became the first approved for pediatric use of this combination, as noted in a review of that approval [4][2]. The marketer cited in that review is VIVUS [2].

The two components have separate histories. Phentermine, a norepinephrine and dopamine releasing agent chemically related to amphetamine, was approved by the FDA in 1959 as an appetite suppressant and is licensed for short-term use alone.[30] Topiramate, discovered in 1979 at McNeil Pharmaceuticals and sold from 1996 as an anticonvulsant, is mainly used for epilepsy and migraine prevention, and weight loss is among its recognised side effects.[31] Qsymia was designed to combine the two so that each is used at lower amounts than it would be alone.[2][8]

Reviews describe it as one of the more effective of the older oral obesity drugs, although network meta-analyses of drugs place incretin-based injections ahead of it [7][8][9][10]. Studies have also examined it in binge-eating disorder and bulimia, adolescents and after bariatric surgery [3][14][16].
Topiramate is associated with birth defects and the combination is reviewed for use in women of reproductive age with obesity [1].

Appearance-minded users approach it as a way to lose body fat. Wikipedia reports highest-dose weight loss of about 10 to 11 percent in trials against 1 to 2 percent on placebo,[22] a magnitude that visibly changes facial and body shape; the drug is prescription-only in the US and a Schedule IV controlled substance.[22]

paras: Qsymia is indicated for chronic weight management as an adjunct to a reduced-calorie diet and physical activity in adults with obesity or overweight with comorbidity, and since 2022 for adolescents aged 12 and older [11][2]. Developers have also pursued sleep apnoea, type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease [2].

Appearance relevance runs through weight loss. Leaner faces and bodies follow sustained fat loss, and people who use prescription appetite drugs often describe goals such as visible abdominal definition. On T Nation, a poster described his wife, who wanted visible abs, suggesting phentermine after a long diet left him constantly hungry,[27] another recounted a coworker losing weight on phentermine with injections,[28] and a third wrote that a GLP-1 drug worked best for stopping constant thoughts of food after trying ephedrine, phentermine and ADHD medications.[29]
It is discussed in reviews of obesity drugs as an option producing substantial but not bariatric-surgery-scale weight loss.[5][6]

A 2024 network meta-analysis in The Lancet covered 132 randomised trials and 48,209 participants and reported that all weight-lowering drugs reduced bodyweight against lifestyle modification alone, with high to moderate certainty evidence placing phentermine-topiramate as the most effective in lowering weight.[23] A 2025 Nature Medicine network meta-analysis of 56 trials (only two of phentermine/topiramate) reported all obesity drugs beat placebo, with more than 10 percent total weight loss for semaglutide and tirzepatide.[25] A 2024 JAMA review groups phentermine-topiramate with naltrexone-bupropion as centrally acting drugs associated with constipation in about 20 percent of patients.[24] The American Gastroenterological Association's 2022 guideline lists phentermine-topiramate extended-release among the agents it assessed and strongly recommends pharmacotherapy alongside lifestyle intervention for eligible adults.[26] Wikipedia reports highest-dose weight loss of about 10-11 percent versus 1-2 percent on placebo and notes discontinuation is recommended if less than 3 percent is lost after three months.[22]

Phase 3 development included trials of controlled-release phentermine plus topiramate in overweight and obese adults; reviews summarize these as showing greater weight loss than placebo, with dose-related effects [7][8][9][11]. Smaller studies include a crossover randomized trial in binge-eating disorder and bulimia nervosa [3], a pilot in binge-eating disorder [15], a study of kidney function [12], a phase 4 study in 232 obese patients [13], a trial among wearable-tracker users [19], and studies in adolescents [14][20][17]. A trial as an adjunct to surgery in the superobese was also registered [16]. Pharmacokinetic work covers hepatic impairment [21].

Reviews and the approval record discuss paresthesia, dry mouth, constipation, insomnia and cognitive effects, as well as increased heart rate [7][8][11]. Topiramate use in pregnancy is associated with oral clefts, and reproductive-age reviews address the combination's contraception requirements [1]. Phentermine's own cardiovascular warnings are described on its article page.

Wikipedia lists common effects of tingling, dizziness, altered taste, insomnia, constipation and dry mouth, serious risks of suicidal thoughts and behaviour, abuse potential and increased resting heart rate, and label warnings on glaucoma, mood and sleep disorders and metabolic acidosis.[22] Contraindications include pregnancy, glaucoma, hyperthyroidism and use with or within 14 days of MAO inhibitors; pregnancy tests and contraception are required because first-trimester topiramate exposure raises the risk of oral clefts.[22]

Topiramate's cognitive effects, such as slowed thinking and word-finding difficulty, are among the reasons 11 to 28 percent of patients stop taking it, according to Wikipedia; it can also reduce the effectiveness of estrogen-containing oral contraceptives and may impair heat regulation.[31] Phentermine is contraindicated with a history of cardiovascular disease or drug abuse, and its common effects include fast heartbeat, raised blood pressure, insomnia and restlessness.[30]

The combination is designed to decrease appetite and increase satiety through two mechanisms, with phentermine acting as a sympathomimetic and topiramate acting on several neural targets [2][8]. Pharmacodynamic studies in obese patients have examined peripheral effects [18].

Phentermine acts as a releasing agent for norepinephrine and dopamine, with weaker effects on serotonin, and has an elimination half-life of about 20 to 25 hours, with most of a dose excreted unchanged in urine.[30] Topiramate's mechanism is not fully understood; proposed targets include voltage-gated sodium channels, calcium channels, GABA-A and AMPA/kainate receptors and carbonic anhydrase enzymes, the last of which may relate to metabolic acidosis and kidney stones.[31] Wikipedia's Qsymia article states that the exact mechanism of the combination for weight loss is unknown.[22]

Topiramate and phentermine each predate the combination by decades: phentermine was approved in 1959 and topiramate was first sold in 1996, with US generics from 2006.[30][31] Phentermine was widely used in the 1990s with fenfluramine in the 'fen-phen' regimen, which was withdrawn in 1997 after heart-valve problems; Wikipedia attributes the valve disease and pulmonary hypertension to fenfluramine rather than phentermine.[30]

The combination was developed by Vivus as VI-0521 and Qnexa.[4][2][12] According to Wikipedia, Vivus submitted its application in 2009; the FDA issued a complete response letter in 2010 citing long-term data, heart rate, cardiovascular events and birth defects, then approved the resubmitted drug in 2012 with US availability starting that September, together with a REMS programme and a required post-approval cardiovascular outcomes trial. European approval was denied in October 2012 over safety concerns.[22] The FDA issued a warning about topiramate and cleft lip and palate in 2011.[31] The 2022 approval for pediatric patients aged 12 and older followed.[2]

Qsymia is a US Schedule IV controlled substance and carries a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS) programme.[22] Newer injectable incretin drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide have since overtaken it in public attention, and network analyses report larger weight loss for them.[25] In bodybuilding forums, users discuss appetite suppressants for cutting weight toward physique goals and compare phentermine with GLP-1 drugs,[27][29] reflecting use of the drug class in contexts beyond its labelled indication.

Phentermine alone was the 168th most prescribed medication in the US in 2023, with over 3 million prescriptions, and is a Schedule IV controlled substance internationally; the UK withdrew it from the market in 2000.[30] Topiramate was the 71st most prescribed US medication in 2023.[31] Commentary in bodybuilding forums often compares appetite suppressants with GLP-1 drugs, reflecting how the weight-loss drug field shifted after semaglutide and tirzepatide arrived.[29][25]

timeline.event: FDA approves phentermine as an appetite suppressant.[30]
Topiramate discovered at McNeil Pharmaceuticals; sold from 1996.[31]
Fen-phen (phentermine plus fenfluramine) withdrawn after heart-valve problems.[30]
Vivus submits its application for the combination.[22]
FDA declines to approve the combination over long-term data and safety concerns.[22]
FDA approves Qsymia (US availability from September); EU approval denied in October.[4][22]
First pediatric approval of the combination (July).[2]
Lancet network meta-analysis of 132 trials ranks phentermine-topiramate among the most effective non-injectable options.[23]

lore.intro: On T Nation, appetite suppressants including phentermine are discussed in the context of cutting body fat for a leaner physique and compared with newer GLP-1 drugs.[27][29]

claims.claim: Appetite suppressants make it easier to get visibly lean on a cut.
claims.believers: Posters describe prescription suppressants as a way to cope with constant hunger while dieting toward visible abs.[27][29]
claims.experts: Trials report about 10 to 11 percent weight loss at the highest dose versus 1 to 2 percent on placebo.[22]

claims.claim: GLP-1 drugs have made older pills like Qsymia obsolete.
claims.believers: A 2021 poster wrote that a GLP-1 drug worked best for stopping food thoughts after trying other stimulants and appetite agents.[29]
claims.experts: A 2025 Nature Medicine meta-analysis reported more than 10 percent total weight loss for semaglutide and tirzepatide, above other classes.[25]

claims.believers: Appetite-suppressant discussions on bodybuilding forums weigh side effects against the appetite control and weight loss users want.[27][29]
claims.experts: Cognitive slowing and word-finding trouble are documented effects and a common reason for discontinuation.[31][8]

card.summary: Once-daily phentermine plus topiramate capsule with clear weight loss over placebo, though behind GLP-1 injections, and a pregnancy risk.
card.note: Topiramate component linked to birth defects; Rx-only.

quick.overview:
Qsymia pairs phentermine, a stimulant appetite suppressant, with topiramate, an anticonvulsant, in a single daily capsule. It was approved in 2012 and extended to adolescents in 2022.

Phase 3 trials show more weight loss than placebo, but newer injectable drugs outperform it in comparative analyses.
quick.mechanism: Phentermine raises norepinephrine release to reduce hunger, while topiramate is thought to add satiety and reduce appetite through other brain pathways. Together they are designed to lower appetite more than either alone.
quick.risks: Reported effects include tingling, dry mouth, constipation, insomnia and cognitive slowing, and increased heart rate. Topiramate in pregnancy is associated with oral clefts. Prescription-only.

angle.text: Qsymia is a prescription weight-management drug. Its appearance payoff comes through sustained weight loss, which changes facial fullness and body shape; in trials the highest dose produced roughly 10 to 11 percent weight loss against 1 to 2 percent on placebo.[22]
